source.title: Features have life history. And we should care
source.authors: P. Stecher; Sandro Radovanovi'c; Vlasta Sikimić; Reinhard Kahle

page_placements.theme: Feature families, containment and co-activation modules within a single SAE

record.tranche_reason: The study measures hierarchically related SAE features and their decoder geometry, and argues that its scaffold relationships are mostly predictive rather than taxonomic. It does not vary SAE dictionary size.
record.gate_note: The study uses a fixed expansion factor of 64 and tracks independently trained SAEs across training checkpoints. It does not test whether increasing dictionary size splits a feature. Its top-token overlap analysis is an absorption-related proxy, not a direct test of whether a parent fails to fire when a child takes over.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. It trains fixed-size (expansion 64) top-k SAEs at training checkpoints and builds a cross-layer containment DAG among persistent features. It never varies dictionary size or compares SAE objectives. It never checks whether a parent latent fails to fire where a child fires. Its hierarchy is firing-token containment between features in different layers' SAEs, a related but different construct from split-feature families (V3). Its top-8 token-overlap 'absorption vs predictive' analysis cites Chanin et al. but does not measure absorption as V4 defines it. These findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that about 50 persistent carriers form an early-assembled scaffold, largely fixed in the first 1% of training. Jointly ablating these carriers costs more than count-matched controls. Carrier identity is predictable from step-1k firing patterns (AUC 0.80/0.83). The scaffold recruits 64%/53% of active features into its hierarchy by convergence. Training is consistent with a two-phase account: selection early, then calibration of decoder geometry. They describe scaffold edges as compositional/predictive rather than taxonomic.
record.recipe_differences: Top-k SAEs with fixed expansion factor 64 are trained independently at checkpoints and matched across training; the study tracks feature life histories and containment rather than varying dictionary size to measure splitting.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports different hierarchy coverage and breadth ratios at Pythia-160M versus Pythia-410M. Its absorption-related conclusion depends on the top-8 token overlap criterion and the taxonomic subset-ratio threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Persistent SAE features form a cross-layer firing-containment DAG covering 64% (160M) / 53% (410M) of active features at convergence. Contained features fire more narrowly, and edge decoder columns are more aligned than nulls (45×/12×/4.3× at 410M).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features tracked across training organise into a cross-layer containment hierarchy seeded by early-born broad features, with above-null decoder alignment along containment edges.

fits_no_version.finding: 99.6% of scaffold containment edges have top-8 token overlap below 0.5 (mean 0.056), versus 95.2% of non-scaffold edges; authors call these predictive rather than taxonomic.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Containment relations among SAE features mostly reflect overlapping predictive context rather than strict token-set subsumption, by a top-token overlap proxy; this does not measure absorption directly.

record.problems: The study uses one training corpus and four sampled layers at each of two model scales; its authors state that generalisation to other architectures, corpora, and scales remains open. The evidence is described as correlational. The reported containment hierarchy and decoder alignment are not a dictionary-size splitting test, and the absorption analysis uses top-token overlap rather than measuring parent and child firing directly.

untested.parts: No dictionary-size variation; expansion fixed at 64.
No splitting test in larger models or open SAE releases; Pythia-160M/410M with own SAEs only.
No families formed by dictionary-size splitting; the hierarchy studied is cross-layer firing-token containment among checkpoint-matched features.
No measurement of parent latents failing to fire where children fire, nor of size/sparsity changes.
No comparison of latents across dictionary sizes or test for novel latents.
No comparison of SAE objectives (e.g., Matryoshka) or test of whether the objective produces splitting.

record.verdict_notes: The record labelled V3 as tested, but the hierarchy is cross-layer containment among features tracked over training at a fixed dictionary size. It is not splitting, so all verdicts are withdrawn. Table 2's caption says '4× expansion SAE' while the method states expansion 64, an internal inconsistency. Decoder cosines are computed between decoder columns of SAEs trained on different layers, which complicates any geometric 'family' reading.

versions.untested_parts: No SAE dictionary-size sweep or measurement of a coarse feature being replaced by finer features.
No large-model or open-release SAE dictionary-size comparison; the study uses Pythia-160M and Pythia-410M with fixed SAE expansion factor.

The study measures containment hierarchies and decoder alignment for features developing across training, not families formed by dictionary-size splitting; it does not establish that the hierarchy mirrors a semantic concept hierarchy.

The study does not measure whether a parent fails to fire where a child fires, or whether changing SAE size or sparsity fixes that effect. Its top-token overlap analysis is only an absorption-related proxy.
No comparison of larger- and smaller-dictionary latents or test of whether larger dictionaries add novel latents.
No comparison of SAE objectives, including Matryoshka SAEs, or test of whether the objective produces splitting.

relation.reason: Engages with feature absorption only in one Appendix A paragraph (top-8 overlap; scaffold called compositional, not taxonomic). It runs no test of any feature-splitting version.

tranche.reason: Fixed-size (expansion 64) top-k SAEs across training checkpoints; no dictionary-size variation, no split-feature families, and no test of a parent failing to fire. Its cross-layer containment edges are a different construct from V3's split-feature families.

source_check.notes: No verdicts, which is correct: the study tracks feature life histories and cross-layer firing-containment among persistent carriers, not splitting with dictionary size. The 160M decoder-cosine row has only a rank ordering, no numbers.

statements.correction: No change needed. Optional precision: coverage = active features reachable from persistent carriers; 99.6%/95.2% are at Pythia-160M.
statements.problem: All numbers match the text: 64% (160M) and 53% (410M) carrier sub-DAG coverage at step 143k; 45x/12x/4.3x median absolute decoder cosine above three nulls at 410M; 99.6% of 916 scaffold edges predictive (top-8 subset ratio < 0.5, mean 0.056) vs 95.2% of 3,409 non-scaffold edges. The 99.6%/95.2% figures are for the 51-carrier (Pythia-160M) scaffold; the statement gives no scale but does not misattribute one.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Scaffold hierarchies in Pythia-160M and Pythia-410M at step 143k
reader_labels.reason: The carrier sub-DAG covers 64% and 53% of active features, respectively, with lower firing breadth inside the hierarchy (R3–R6); scaffold-edge decoder directions are more aligned than the reported null pairings (R1–R2). These results support a hierarchy with geometric alignment in this setting.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The study reports that 99.6% of scaffold edges are predictive rather than taxonomic under its top-token overlap criterion; this limits interpreting the measured hierarchy as a strict taxonomic concept hierarchy (R7).
